newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Estonian president says Russia still "evil empire".
newsitem.headline: Estonian president says Russia still "evil empire".

text.p: Estonian President Lennart Meri said on Wednesday Russia was still an "evil empire" for resisting NATO expansion and urged former Soviet republics and Warsaw Pact states to challenge it.

"Let us adhere to our agreements...and present an uncompromising challenge to the empire of evil, or more accurately, to the shadow of its former self which for its own purposes did not before, nor would today, relinquish its hold on anyone," Meri said.

Meri, who made the remark during a speech to students at an economics university, did not mention Russia by name but used the same terminology U.S. president Ronald Reagan used when he denounced the former Soviet Union as an "evil empire".
Meri, on a three-day visit, said he had held talks with Hungarian officials about plans by formerly communist Eastern and Central European states to join NATO and the EU.
NATO and Russia agreed a deal on Wednesday intended to sweep away Moscow's concerns over the expansion of the Western defence alliance. Meri spoke before the agreement in Moscow was made public.
A NATO summit in Madrid in July is expected to invite Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic to be the first former east bloc states to join NATO.

The change is likely to be grudgingly accepted by Russia, but diplomats have said Moscow would oppose membership for the Baltic states which were part of the Soviet Union and not just Warsaw Pact members.

Meri told Reuters that he and Hungarian officials had discussed NATO enlargement and had found points in common, even though Hungary is expected to be admitted in the first round of expansion while Estonia and the other Baltic states of Latvia and Lithuania are likely to be asked to wait.
"Having the same goals but not being in an Olympic stadium means that we are helping each other," Meri said.
Asked if he thought Estonia would be asked to join NATO in the near future, he said: "It's not a question of Olympic games, it is a long process."
Meri, who is accompanied by a number of business people, also talked about Hungary's and Estonia's shared cultural heritage based on both peoples speaking a Finno-Ugric tongue.
